Return now to unconstrained optimization problems. Say that we have
reason to expect that over a particular region $R$, the distribution
$p^\beta(x)$ has values approximately $\kappa$ times as small as its
value over $X \setminus R$. It would be nice to reflect this insight
in our parametrization of $q$, that is, to parametrize $q$ in a way that
makes it easy to match it to $p^\beta(x)$ accurately. We can do this
using a binary-valued function $\Phi$ and the approaches presented above.

To illustrate this, define ${\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta}$ as above and
choose the objective function ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}(\theta) =$
KL$(p^\beta \;||\; {\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta})$, where $ (x) =
 $ over $R$, and equals 1 over $X R$. Note that we use
$p^\beta$ in this ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$, not $p^\beta_\Phi$,
which is what we used for constrained optimization. This is because
our goal now is simply to find a $q_\theta$ that matches
$p^\beta(x)$. There are no additional aspects to the problem involving
feasibility regions that have no a priori relation to $G(x)$. 
Then working through the algebra, the $q_\theta$ that minimizes this
objective is given by the ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$ that minimizes
\begin{eqnarray}
-\int dx p^\beta(x)  {\mbox{ln}}[{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)] \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx'
{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')
\Phi(x')] &=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^\beta \;||\; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}) \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')
\Phi(x')]  \nonumber \\
&=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^\beta \;||\; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}) \;+\ \nonumber \\
&& \;\;\;\;\;{\mbox{ln}}[\int dx'_R \; \kappa {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x') +  \int dx'_{X
\setminus R} \; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')] . \nonumber \\
&&
\end{eqnarray}
The logarithm on the right-hand side is a `correction' to $pq$
distance from $p^\beta$ to ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$, a correction that
pushes ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$ $away$ from regions where $\Phi(x) = 1$
(assuming $\kappa < 1$). To use immediate sampling with this
parametrization scheme, once we find the ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$ that
minimizes the sum of $pq$ distance plus that correction term, we would
set $h$ to the distribution (proportional to)
${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)\Phi(x)$. So we would generate our new samples
from ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)\Phi(x)$, for example by
subsampling. In practice, $\Phi(x)$ for this unconstrained
case would not be provided by an oracle. Instead we would typically
have to estimate it. We could do that for example by using a
regression to form a fit to samples of $p^\beta(x)$ and then use that
regression to define the region $R$.

이제 제약이 없는 최적화 문제로 돌아가 보겠습니다. 특정 영역 $R$에서 분포 $p^\beta(x)$의 값이 $X \setminus R$에서의 값의 약 $\kappa$배 작을 것으로 예상된다고 가정해 보겠습니다. 이러한 통찰을 $q$의 매개변수화에 반영하는 것이 좋습니다. 즉, $p^\beta(x)$와 정확하게 일치하도록 $q$를 매개변수화하는 방법을 찾는 것입니다. 우리는 이진 값 함수 $\Phi$와 위에서 제시한 접근 방식을 사용하여 이를 수행할 수 있습니다.

이를 설명하기 위해, 위에서 정의한 대로 ${\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta}$를 정의하고, 목적 함수 ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}(\theta) = \text{KL}(p^\beta \;||\; {\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta})$를 선택합니다. 여기서 $ (x) = $는 $R$에서 정의되고, $X R$에서는 1로 설정됩니다. 우리는 이 ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$에서 $p^\beta$를 사용하고, 제약 최적화에 사용했던 $p^\beta_\Phi$는 사용하지 않는다는 점에 유의해야 합니다. 이는 현재 우리의 목표가 단순히 $p^\beta(x)$와 일치하는 $q_\theta$를 찾는 것이기 때문입니다. $G(x)$와 사전적으로 관련이 없는 타당성 영역과 관련된 추가적인 측면은 없습니다. 그러면 대수를 통해 작업을 진행하면, 이 목적을 최소화하는 $q_\theta$는 다음을 최소화하는 ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$로 주어집니다.

\begin{eqnarray}
-\int dx p^\beta(x)  {\mbox{ln}}[{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)] \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx'
{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')
\Phi(x')] &=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^\beta \;||\; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}) \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')
\Phi(x')]  \nonumber \\
&=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^\beta \;||\; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}) \;+\ \nonumber \\
&& \;\;\;\;\;{\mbox{ln}}[\int dx'_R \; \kappa {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x') +  \int dx'_{X
\setminus R} \; {{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x')] . \nonumber \\
&&
\end{eqnarray}

우변의 로그는 $p^\beta$에서 ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$까지의 $pq$ 거리의 '수정'으로, $\Phi(x) = 1$인 영역에서 ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$를 멀어지게 하는 수정입니다(여기서 $\kappa < 1$이라고 가정합니다). 이 매개변수화 방식으로 즉각적인 샘플링을 사용하기 위해, $pq$ 거리와 그 수정 항의 합을 최소화하는 ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$를 찾으면, 우리는 $h$를 분포 (비례하여) ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)\Phi(x)$로 설정합니다. 따라서 우리는 예를 들어 서브샘플링을 통해 ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x)\Phi(x)$에서 새로운 샘플을 생성할 것입니다. 실제로 이 제약이 없는 경우의 $\Phi(x)$는 오라클에 의해 제공되지 않을 것입니다. 대신 우리는 일반적으로 이를 추정해야 합니다. 예를 들어, 회귀를 사용하여 $p^\beta(x)$ 샘플에 맞추고, 그 회귀를 사용하여 영역 $R$을 정의할 수 있습니다.

summary.content: 이 섹션에서는 제약이 없는 최적화 문제를 다루며, 특정 영역에서 분포 \( p^\beta(x) \)의 값을 다른 영역에 비해 약 \(\kappa\) 배 작게 예상할 수 있는 경우, 이를 매개변수화하여 \( q \)와 \( p^\beta(x) \)를 정확하게 일치시키는 방법을 제시합니다. 목표는 \( p^\beta(x) \)와 일치하는 \( q_\theta \)를 찾는 것이며, 이를 위해 KL 발산을 사용한 목적 함수를 정의합니다. 최적화 과정에서 \( \Phi(x) \)를 통해 \( q_\theta \)를 조정하고, 최종적으로 새로운 샘플을 생성하기 위해 \( \tilde{q}_\theta(x)\Phi(x) \)를 사용합니다. 실험적으로는 \( \Phi(x) \)를 오라클이 제공하지 않기 때문에 회귀 분석을 통해 추정해야 합니다.

sections.content:
Not all PC objectives can be cast as an integral transform. Properly
speaking, the choice of objective should be set by how the final
$q_\theta$ will be used. For instance, the concept of expected improvement suggested by ~ , and used by , considers an objective (to be maximized) given by $\max(G_{\mathrm{bc}} - G(x), 0)$, where $G_{\mathrm{bc}}$ is the best of all the current samples, $\min_i \{G(x^i)\}$. This means that at each step we will take a single sample, and want to maximize the improvement. This is a simplification; even though the next sample may yield any improvement, it may be informative, so that we get a good sample ten steps later. A less simplistic objective is the following: 

In blackbox optimization, no matter how many calls to the (factual) oracle we make, we will ultimately choose the best $x$ (as far as the associated $G$ value is concerned) out of all the ones that were fed to the oracle during the course of the entire run. Our true goal in BO is to have the $G$ associated with $that$ best $x$ be as small as possible. For a discussion of distributions of extremal values, see ~ . 

Given that $q_\theta$ varies over the run in a way that we do not 
know beforehand, how can one approximate this goal as minimizing an 
objective function that is well-defined at all points during the run? 
One way to do this is to assume that there is some integer $N$ such 
that, simultaneously, 

- It is likely that the best $x$ will be one of the final $N$ 
calls to the oracle during the run; 

- It is likely that $q_\theta$ will not vary much during the 
generation of those final $N$ samples. 

Under (2) we can approximate the $q_\theta$'s that are used to 
generate the final $N$ calls as all being equal to some canonical 
$q_\theta$. Under (1), our goal then becomes finding the canonical 
$q_\theta$ that, when sampled $N$ times, produces a set of $x$'s whose 
best element is as good as possible. An obvious variant of this reasoning is to have 
$N$ vary across the run of the entire algorithm, at any iteration $t$ 
being only the number of remaining calls to the oracle that we 
presume will be made. In this variant, one would modify the elite 
objective function to only involve the $N(t)$ remaining samples whose 
$G$ value is better than the best found by iteration $t$. For the case $N=1$, this is 
analogous to the expected improvement idea in~ . Note 
that this variant objective function will change during the run, which 
may cause stability problems. 

In this appendix we make some cursory comments about this objective
function, which we call the elite objective function . We focus
on the use of Bayesian FB techniques with this objective. For a noise-free oracle the CDF for the elite objective is
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{CDF}}(k) &\triangleq& 1 - \int dx^1 \ldots dx^N \; \prod_{i=1}^N
[q_\theta(x^i) \Theta(G(x^i) - k)].
\end{eqnarray}
So the associated density function is
\begin{eqnarray}
f(k) &=& \frac{d \; {\mbox{CDF}}(k)}{dk} \nonumber \\
&=& N q_\theta(k) [\int dx \; q_\theta(x) \Theta(G(x) - k)]^{(N-1)}.
\end{eqnarray}
The associated expectation value, $\int dk \; k f(k)$, is not linear
in $q_\theta$. 

Writing it out, the posterior expected best-of-$K$ value returned by
the oracle when queries are generated by sampling $q_\theta$ is
\begin{eqnarray}
\int dx^1 \ldots dx^K \; \prod_{i=1}^K q_\theta(x^i) \int dG \;
P(G \mid D) \; \int dg^1 \ldots dg^K \prod_{j=1}^K P(g^k \mid x^k, G)
{\mbox{min}}_k \{g^k\}
\label{eq:elite}
\end{eqnarray}
We want the $\theta$ minimizing this. Say we knew the exact posterior
$P(G \mid D)$ and could evaluate the associated integral in
Eq.~ closed-form. In this case there would be need for
the parametric machine learning techniques used in the text. In particular
there would be no need for regularization --- an analogous role is
played by the prior $P(G)$ underlying $P(G \mid D)$.

When we cannot evaluate the integral in closed form we must
approximate it. To illustrate this, as in Sec.~ ,
for simplicity consider a single-valued oracle $G$. This reduces
Eq.~ to
\begin{eqnarray} 
\int dx^1 \ldots dx^K \; \prod_{i=1}^K q_\theta(x^i) \int dG \; 
P(G \mid D) {\mbox{min}}_k \{G(x^k)\}. 
\label{eq:elite_single_valued} 
\end{eqnarray} 

(The analogous FB MCO equation for objective functions involving a
single integral Eq.~ ; here the single
`$x$' in that equation is replaced with a set of $K$ $x$'s sampled
from $q_{\theta}$.) To approximate this integral we draw $N_T$
sample-vectors of $K$ $x$'s each, using a sampling distribution
$h_c(x)$ to do so. At the same time we draw $N_T$ fictitious oracles
from some sampling distribution $H$ over oracles.

To simplify notation, let ${\vec{x}}$ indicate such a $K$-tuple of
$x$'s. (So for multidimensional $X$, ${\vec{x}}$ is actually a
matrix.) Also write
\begin{eqnarray}
h_c({\vec{x}}) &\triangleq& \prod_{i=1}^K {h_c}(x^k), \nonumber \\
q_\theta({\vec{x}}) &\triangleq& \prod_{i=1}^K q_\theta(x^k), \nonumber \\
G({\vec{x}}) &\triangleq& (G(x^1), \ldots, G(x^K)). 
\end{eqnarray}

With this notation, the estimate based on fictitious samples
introduced in Sec.~ becomes In practice
there might be more efficient sampling procedures than
Eq.~ . For example, one could form $NK$ samples of
${h_c}(x)$ and $N$ samples of $H(G)$, to get two sets, which one then
subsamples many times, to get pairs $[{\vec{x}}, G({\vec{x}})]$. 
\begin{eqnarray}
\sum_{i = 1}^N
	\prod_{j=i}^K \frac{q_\theta(x^j_i)}{{h_c}(x^j_i)} \frac{P(G_i \mid D)}{H(G_i)}
{\mbox{min}}_{k=1,\ldots K} \{G_i(x^k_i)\} .
\label{eq:elite_sum}
\end{eqnarray}

As discussed in Sec.~ , it is often good to set
$H(G)$ to be as close to $P(G \mid D)$ as possible. So for example if
we assume a Gaussian process model, typically we can set $H(G_i) =
P(G_i D)$, and then directly sample $H$ to get the values of one
$G_i$ at the $K$ separate points $x^j_i$. Alternatively, we can first
form a fit $\phi(x)$ to the data in $D$. Next, for each of $N$ samples
${\vec{x}}_i$, sample a colored (correlated) noise process over the
$K$ points \ ${\vec{x}}_i$\ to get $K$ real numbers.

Finally, add those $K$ numbers to the corresponding values
$\{\phi({\vec{x}}_i^j) : j = 1, \ldots, K\}$. This gives our desired
sample of \ $G_i({\vec{x}}_i)$\ .

To illustrate the foregoing, suppose $K = 1$, and that we have no
regularization on $q_\theta$. Then, in general, the sum in
Eq.~ is minimized by a $q_\theta$ that is a delta
function about that data point $x^1_i$ with the best associated value
$G_i(x^1_i) / {h_c}(x^1_i)$. However for $K > 1$, even without
regularization, the optimal $q_\theta$ is not a delta function,
in general. This suboptimality of a delta function $q_\theta$
is similar to the suboptimality of having all $K$ pulls in a
multi-armed bandit problem be pulls of the same arm. In addition to the regularization-based argument in the text, this gives a
more formal reason why the optimal $q_\theta$ should not be infinitely
peaked.

When $K > 1$, the peakedness of $q_\theta$ parallels the peakedness of
another non-negative function over $x$'s, namely $P(G : G(x) 
is minimized at x D)$. However, if we run a few iterations of
FB MCO with the elite objective, then $D$ grows, and so $P(G : G(x)
 is minimized at x D)$ gets increasingly peaked over
$x$'s. (Intuitively, the larger $D$ is, the more confident we are
about $G$, and consequently the more confident we are about what
regions of $x$'s minimize $G$.) Accordingly, $q_\theta$ gets
increasingly peaked as the algorithm progresses. 

Note that this happens even though there is no external annealing
schedule. This reflects the fact that the elite objective has no
hyperparameter or regularization parameter like the $\beta$ that
appears in both the $pq$ and $qp$ objective functions.

summary.content: 이 섹션에서는 블랙박스 최적화에서의 엘리트 목표 함수에 대해 논의하고 있다. 최적화의 목표는 최종적으로 오라클에 제공된 샘플 중에서 가장 좋은 $x$를 선택하는 것이며, 이를 위해 $q_\theta$를 적절히 설정해야 한다. 저자는 $N$개의 최종 호출에서 $q_\theta$가 크게 변하지 않을 것이라는 가정을 통해, 최적의 $q_\theta$를 찾는 방법을 제안한다. 또한, 이 목표 함수는 알고리즘이 진행됨에 따라 변화하며, 데이터가 증가함에 따라 $q_\theta$의 피크가 점점 더 뚜렷해지는 경향이 있음을 설명한다.

The following example illustrates the foregoing for the case of
Gaussian $\pi$, where only moments of $\pi$ up to order 2 matter.

To illustrate the foregoing, consider the
simple case where there are only two $\phi$'s, $\phi^1$ and $\phi^2$.
Suppose that $U$ and $X$ are such that $\pi$ is a two-dimensional
Gaussian. Write $\pi$'s mean as $\mu$. Say that one of $\pi$'s
principal axes is parallel to the diagonal line, $l_1 =
l_2$ (that is, one of the eigenvectors of $ $'s covariance
matrix is parallel to the diagonal, and one is orthogonal to the
diagonal). Write the standard deviation of $\pi$ along that diagonal
axis as $\sigma_A$, and write the standard deviation along the other,
orthogonal axis as $\sigma_B$.

Since $\pi$'s covariance matrix has identical diagonal entries, and
since the trace of that matrix is preserved under rotations, those
entries are both $\frac{1}{2}[\sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}]$. Since the
determinant is preserved, and since $\sigma_A$ is the variance
parallel to the diagonal, this in turn means that $\pi$'s (identical)
off-diagonal entries are $ 1 2 [ _A^ 2 -
 _B^ 2 ]$. The probability that MCO will choose $ ^1$ is the
integral of $\pi$ over the half-plane where $\phi^1 \le \phi^2$:
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{Pr}}({{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^2) > {{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^1) ) &=&
\erf(\frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{\sigma_B \sqrt{2}}) .
\end{eqnarray}

Next, define
\begin{eqnarray}
\Delta L &\equiv&  {\mathscr{L}}(\phi^1) - {\mathscr{L}}(\phi^2), \nonumber \\
\Delta b &\equiv& [\mu_1 - {\mathscr{L}}(\phi^1)] \;\;-\;\; [\mu_2 -
{\mathscr{L}}(\phi^2)] \nonumber \\ 
	&=& [\mu_1 - \mu_2] - \Delta L .
\end{eqnarray}
So the difference in the value of the loss function between the two
$\phi$'s is $\Delta L$, and the the difference in the biases of the
two estimators ${{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^1)$ and ${{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^2)$ is $ 
b$. Note also that the variances of the two estimators are the same,
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{Var}}[{\mathscr{L}}(\phi^1)] \;\;=\;\; {\mbox{Var}}[{\mathscr{L}}(\phi^2)] \;\;=\;\; 
\frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2}.
\end{eqnarray}
So if we shrink the variance of either of the estimators, then we
shrink an upper bound on $\sigma_B$. 

For this case of a fixed set of $\phi$'s, it is illuminating to
consider the difference between expected loss under a particular MCO
algorithm and minimal expected loss over all $\phi$'s, that is, the risk
of the MCO algorithm. Assuming $\Delta L < 0$, it is given by
\begin{eqnarray}
[{\mbox{Pr}}[{{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^2) > {{\hat{\mathscr{L}}}}(\phi^1 )]\;-\;
\Theta[{\mathscr{L}}(\phi^2) - {\mathscr{L}}(\phi^1)] ] \;\times \;
[{\mathscr{L}}(\phi^1) \;-\; {\mathscr{L}}(\phi^2)] \nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
\begin{eqnarray}
&=& \nonumber
\end{eqnarray}

\begin{eqnarray}
[\erf(\frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{\sigma_B \sqrt{2}}) - \Theta(\Delta b +
\mu_2 - \mu_1) ] \; \times \; [\mu_1 - \mu_2 - \Delta b] . 
\label{eq:risk}
\end{eqnarray}
Say that $\Delta b = 0$. Then Eq.~ shows that so long as
$\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, as $\sigma_B \rightarrow 0$ risk goes to its
minimal possible value of zero. So everything else being equal,
shrinking the variance of either estimator reduces risk, essentially
minimizing it. Alternatively, if we leave the variances of the two
estimators unchanged, but increase their covariance,
$\frac{1}{2}[\sigma^2_A - \sigma_B^2]$, then $\sigma_A$ will increase,
while $\sigma_B$ must shrink. So again, the risk will get reduced.
For the more general, non-Gaussian case, the high order moments may
also come into play.

Then since $d$ is finite, we run a risk of over-fitting, and
therefore, as usual in supervised learning, must regularize. Moreover,
the more data we have --- the bigger $d$ is --- the less
regularization is needed. So ... iterative techniques are just
sequences of regularizers, with weakening regularization as $d$ grows!

This tells us exactly how to set the free parameters in the
regularizations of any such sequence. How does one choose the

***

 DHW: Get rid of this paragraph? One potential difficulty with
this approach is that when descending $G_\beta(q)$ over $q$, one
might encounter a $q$ such that the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ V_i
\;||\; q)$ contains many constraints $i$. Now in such a case, since
the overall problem is convex, we know that there is some direction
$\delta q$ in which we could infinitesimally move $q$ that would lower
all those (tight) constraints simultaneously. In other words, there
is a $\delta q$ having non-zero dot product with the $q$-gradients of
all the members of the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ V_i \;||\;
q)$. Moreover, finding such a $ q$ is just a Linear Programming
(LP) problem. In particular, we can use LP techniques to find the
$\delta q$ that has minimal dot product with the $q$-gradient
$\frac{\partial}{\partial q} {\mathbb{E}}_{q,{\mathscr{G}}}(g)$ while having non-zero dot product
with the $q$-gradients of all the members of the set argmax$_i$
KL$(p^\beta V_i \;||\; q)$. Once we have solved for this $\delta q$,
we could take a small step along it, and then again find the set
argmax$_i$ KL$(p^\beta V_i \;||\; q)$ to continue the descent
process. As an alternative, one could address the difficulty
by temporarilly approximating $G_\beta(q)$, for example as
$[ _i \; ( KL (p^ V_i
\;||\; q))^m]^ 1/m $ for a large $m$. 

***

$ $

 ii) Constraint satisfaction 

$ $

 DHW: The following won't work. The reason is that KL distance
from $q$ to (the Boltzmann distribution for) any single $V_i$ will be
minimized by having $q$ proportional to $V_i$. It can't be
proportional to $V_i$ for all $V_i$ though.

In fact, what we want is to have our objective function be minimized
for $q$ a delta function about a feasible $x$. However the KL distance
between any single $V_i$ and that delta-function $q_\theta$ is
infinite (!). We will get a lower value of the objective function if
$q_\theta$ ranges over $x$'s that disagree with at least some of the
constraints. 

Consider using the approach of part (i) in the special case of
constraint satisfaction problems, where $G(x)$ is constant and
therefore irrelevant. In such problems, there is no issue of
`balancing' the conflicting needs that ${\tilde{q}}_\theta$ have as
much as possible of its probability mass on feasible $x$'s and that it
be concentrated on $x$'s with large $p^\beta(x)$. So 
the modification discussed above in which one uses the
objective function KL$(p^\beta_\Phi \; || \; {\tilde{q}}_\theta)$
rather than KL$(p^\beta_\Phi \; || \; {\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta})$
is less problematic for constraint satisfication problems than for
constrained optimization problems.

In constraint satisfication that modification means using
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{KL}}(\frac{\Phi}{\int dx' \Phi(x')} \; || \;
{\tilde{q}}_\theta)
\end{eqnarray}
 rather than
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{KL}}(\frac{\Phi}{\int dx'
\Phi(x')} \; || \; \frac{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}{\int dx' \;
{{\tilde{q}}_\theta}(x') \Phi(x')}).
\end{eqnarray}
Under this modification we don't have the second integral of
Eq.~ pushing ${\tilde{q}}_\theta$ away from
feasible $x$'s. Due to this, the modification may outperform the
original approach, as far as finding a feasible $x$ is
concerned. Indeed, for this constraint satisfaction case, it makes
sense to consider an objective given by a further slight modification,
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathscr{F}}_\Phi(\theta) &\triangleq& {\mbox{KL}}(\frac{e^{-\beta [1 
- \Phi]}}{\int dx'
e^{-\beta \Phi(x')}} \; || \; {{q}}_\theta) \nonumber \\
&\triangleq& {\mbox{KL}}(\rho^{\beta,\Phi} \; || \; {{q}}_\theta)
\label{eq:constr_sat}
\end{eqnarray}
where since we are not using masking to parameterize $q$ there is no
reason any more for a tilde over $q$.

This ${\mathscr{F}}_\Phi$ is just $pq$ distance for a `$G(x)$' set
equal to $1 - \Phi(x)$. So if we believe that in general PC using $pq$
distance will find a good solution to (P4), then we would expect that
using it with the objective function in Eq.~ will
result in a good solution to the problem of finding an $x$ that
minimizes $1 - \Phi(x)$, that is, the problem of finding a feasible $x$.

Now consider the particular case where the constraint function $\Phi$
is given by the intersection of $M$ constraints, where $M$ is very
large. Say that each region in $X$ separately meeting one of the $M$
constraints is substantial, but due to the size of $M$, $\Phi(x) = 1$
only for an extremely small subregion of $X$. In such a situation, it
may be that early in the run all sample $x$'s have $\Phi(x) = 0$. This
would mean that those samples provide no information on how to modify
$q_\theta$ to have it concentrate more on feasible $x$'s.

Intuitively, one way around this problem would be somehow to decompose
$\Phi$ into the $M$ constituent constraints, and address them
separately and simultaneously. Since the feasible region for each
separate constraint is large, even early in the run each of those
constraints $separately$ would consider many sample $x$'s to be
feasible. (The constraints would disagree though on which $x$'s they
consider feasible.) So we might be able to Monte Carlo estimate
feasibility information on the constraints taken separately. The goal
would be to then combine such information from all the constraints, to
solve our overall optimization problem involving all $M$ constraints.

To illustrate how one might do this, return to the case where $X =
 _j X_j$ and each component space $X_j$ is relatively small
and finite (e.g., $X$ is a hypercube). Consider product distributions
$q_\theta$ and for simplicity dispense with the subscript $\theta$,
that is, use the trivial parametrization $\theta = \{q(x) : x \in X\}$.
Write each of the $M$ constraints as a feasibility function $V_i(x)$
that equals 1 if constraint $i$ is satisfied, 0 otherwise. (So
$\Phi(x) \triangleq \prod_{i=1}^M V_i(x)$.) Also define
\begin{eqnarray}
G_\beta(q) &\triangleq& {\mbox{max}}_i [{\mbox{KL}}(\rho^{\beta,V_i} \;||\; q)]  .
\end{eqnarray}

For our product distribution $q$, each $ KL ( ^ , V_i 
\;||\; q)$ is a convex function of $q$. Therefore for fixed $ $,
$G_\beta(q)$ is a convex function of $q$. This means that there are
no spurious local minima of $G_\beta$. Moreover, for any $\beta > 0$,
the $q$ that minimizes $G_\beta(q)$ will have its support restricted
to feasible $x$. So a natural iterative algorithm is to fix $\beta$,
minimize the associated function $ KL ( ^ , V_i \;||\;
q)$ as much as reasonable, and then raise $ $ and repeat, as in
conventional annealing.

This approach can be used either for blackbox optimization or when we
know the full optimization specification, so that there is no
oracle. As an example of its application in the latter domain,
consider a KSAT problem, where each clause of the problem corresponds
to one $V_i$, and each $x_j$ is a single bit. Define $[ ^ ,
V_i ]^j$ as the marginalization of $ ^ , V_i $ onto component
$x_j$. For typical KSAT problems (that is, typical values of K) each such
marginalization can be evaluated closed-form with little communication
overhead. Now consider any term KL$( ^ , V_i 
\;||\; q)$ (one term for each clause $V_i$). That term will be given
by a sum, over all components $x_j$ that occur in clause $i$, of
KL$([\rho^{\beta, V_i}]^j \;||\; q_j)$. (Those components of $x$ are
the only ones on which $V_i(x)$ depends.)

Again, for typical KSAT problems, for every clause $i$ there are few
such $x_j$. That means that if in fact each $[\rho^{\beta, V_i}]^j$
can be easily evaluated, then we can evaluate KL$( ^ , V_i 
\;||\; q)$ in closed form easily for any $q$, as well as its gradient,
etc. Accordingly, we can optimize $G_\beta(q)$ in closed form, for
example using epigraph methods.

As another example of this approach, say that unlike the typical KSAT
problem, we only have oracles for each $V_i$. So we have a blackbox
constraint-satisfaction problem. For such a problem it may make sense
to use immediate sampling to do the optimization. In this approach
each term KL$(\rho^{\beta, V_i} \;||\; q)$ is approximated as a sum,
via importance sampling. (Note that one might to have a different
sample of $x$'s for each $i$). One then does uses that sum to estimate
the optimal $q$, in the usual immediate sampling ways.

This max-based approach can also be helpful when $G(x)$ is not
constant, so we don't have a constraint-satisfication problem. To see
how, say that we ignore $G$ temporarilly, so that our constrained
optimization problem becomes a constraint satisfication problem, with
feasibility function $\Phi$. Run the max-based approach on this
constraint satisfaction problem until we generate a solution
$q_{\theta'}$ with small $pq$ distance to $\rho^{\beta,\Phi}$ for a
large $\beta$. Unlike the $q_\theta$ arising in the approach of part (i)
of this appendix, $q_{\theta'}$ will in general not have its support
restricted to $x$ such that $\Phi(x) = 1$. However it may well assign
high probability to such $x$'s. If that is the case, then generating
samples of ${\tilde{q}}_{\Phi,\theta}$ by subsampling $q_{\theta'}$
according to $\Phi$ should be relatively efficient (that is, should
result in relatively few rejected samples). Accordingly, in running
the constrained optimization approach of part (i), we may want to
initialize ${{\tilde{q}}_\theta}$ to $q_{\theta'}$.

***

$ $

 ) Fictitous sampling for supervised learning 

$ $

In a fully Bayesian approach to the supervised-learning problem, the
`target' stochastic process, which generated the training set $d$ of
Eq.~ , is not completely known. Accordingly, there is
a distribution across all possible targets. That distribution reflects
the information we have concerning the target, which includes in
particular the fact that the training set $d$ was generated by
sampling the target. 

This means that we should replace $P(y \mid x)$ in
Eq.~ with a conditional distribution $P(y 
x,d)$. This gives the following optimization problem:
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{argmin}}_\theta && \int dx \; P(x)[\int dy \; P(y \mid x, d) L(y,
z_\theta(x))] .
\end{eqnarray}
To explicitly delineate the dependence on the target stochastic
process on $d$, let $f$ indicate that target, and with some abuse of
notation write the distribution of outputs $y$ for a given input $x$
and target $f$ as $P(y \mid x, f)$. With this notation our fully
Bayesian treatment of supervised learning becomes the following
optimization problem:
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{argmin}}_\theta && \int dx \; P(x)[\int dy\,df \; P(f \mid d) P(y \mid x, f) L(y,
z_\theta(x))] .
\label{eq:bayes_sup_learn}
\end{eqnarray}

One can use importance-sampling MCO to do this minimization, as
usual. To do this one first chooses a distribution $h_c(x)$ and
$H(f)$. (For simplicity we assume that for any $x, f$, one can sample
$P(y \mid x, f)$ directly.) Then one repeatedly samples $h, H$, and
$P(y \mid x, f)$ to produce a set of triples, \ $(x^i, y^i,
f^i)$\ . Using naive MCO, this transforms our supervised learning
problem into
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mbox{argmin}}_\theta && \sum_i \frac{P(x^i) P(y^i \mid x^i, f^i) L(y^i,
z_\theta(x^i))}{h_c(x_c^i)H(f^i)}
\end{eqnarray}
However for the usual reasons, unless the sample size is very large
one would expect such a minimization to be a poor estimate of the
$\theta$ solving Eq.~ . The natural alternative
to this naive MCO approach is to use PLMCO to solve for $\theta$. Note
that that would mean using supervised learning to help a procedure for
solving a supervised learning problem.

$ $

 ) Comparisons with Conventional Supervised Learning 

$ $

The immediate sampling algorithms explored in the text are indirect
approaches for minimizing Eq.~ . These indirect
approaches are analogs of non-Bayesian approaches to supervised
learning, in which one acknowledges that minimizing
Eq.~ is the ultimate problem of interest, but
one does not directly address that problem. Instead, one invokes
bias-variance arguments, cross-validation, etc. In this appendix, we
have proposed techniques to directly minimize the actual integral of
interest, via importance sampling.

Note though that in conventional Bayesian supervised learning, one is
typically interested in `point predictions' of the value
$z_\theta(x')$ for the $\theta$ minimizing
Eq.~ , for some particular $x'$. Usually, the
minimization is over an extremely broad set of functions
$\{z_\theta\}$, e.g., all twice-differentiable functions from $x$'s to
$y$'s. These factors often mean that one never solves for the optimal
$\theta$ (or the associated full function $z_\theta$) directly, but
just for the value $z_\theta(x')$. This is what is done in Markov
Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian methods, for
example~ .

On the other hand, say one were interested in the optimal $\theta$
rather than a point prediction. For this case fictitious sampling
(based on Markov samplers or importance samplers) using PLMCO rather
than naive MCO would be a natural approach.

***

$ $

 ) Fictitious estimation for Monte Carlo 

$ $

Consider a simple Monte Carlo problem, of estimating the integral
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} &\equiv& \int dx dg \; P(g \mid x, {\mathscr{G}}) g 
\end{eqnarray}
for some potentially stochastic oracle $\mathscr{G}$. (This can be
viewed as a degenerate case of the MCO problem where $\theta$ is
fixed, so we have no optimization to do.) Say we do not know the
oracle ${\mathscr{G}}$. However to help us estimate
${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ we have an information set ${D}$
that gives us information about the oracle. To fix the discussionm, we
can assume that that information set contains samples of the oracle,
as in conventional Monte Carlo estimation.

Adopting the Bayesian decision theory approach, the information set
induces a posterior distribution $P( F _ G 
 D )$. To use that distribution to estimate the integral we
must specify an associated loss function $L$. Let
${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ be our estimate of
${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$. Then $L$ maps the pair
$({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}, {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}})$ to
an associated real-valued `loss'. That loss quantifies how good it
is to make the estimate $ {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ when the
actual value is ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$.

Our goal in Bayesian decision theory is to find the
${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ that minimizes expected loss under
the posterior $P({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {{D}})$
~ . Writing that out, Bayesian decision
theory directs us to find the ${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ that
minimizes
\begin{eqnarray}
\int d{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \; P({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid
{D}) L({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}, {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}})
\end{eqnarray}
In particular, from now on we will assume a quandratic loss
function. For this case our Bayes-optimal estimate of
${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ is just its posterior expected value,
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {D}) &=& \int
d{\mathscr{G}}' \; P({\mathscr{G}}' \mid {D})
{\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}'} \nonumber \\
&=& \int
dx dg d{\mathscr{G}}'  \; P({\mathscr{G}}' \mid {D}) P(g \mid
x, {\mathscr{G}}') g .
\end{eqnarray}

For simplicity, from now on assume (${D}$ tells us that) the
oracle is noise-free. So our posterior expected
${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ becomes
\begin{eqnarray}
\int dx dG' \; P(G' \mid {D}) G(x).
\label{eq:mc_single}
\end{eqnarray}
By Bayes' rule, $P(G D) P(D G)
P(G)$. Single-valuedness of $G$ implies that the likelihood $P(D 
G)$ (and hence $P(G D)$), can only have support on functions
$G(x)$ that go through all the pairs $(x^i,g^i)$ in
$D$. Single-valuedness also makes $P(D \mid G)$ the same delta
function for all functions $G$ that are consistent with $D$, and
therefore, it is only our prior over oracles, $P(G)$, that ranks these
functions. In this way Eq.~ takes into account
prior knowledge concerning $G$. This Bayesian approach also enables us
to incorporate other information that we get from the factual oracle, for
instance, gradients, uncertainty values, etc. Formally, all such
information augments $D$, and therefore affects the $G$-dependence of
the likelihood $P(D \mid G)$.

If it cannot be evaluated closed form we can use MC to estimate the
integral in Eq.~ . One example of how to do that
would be to use MCMC. An alternative is to use importance
sampling. Note that in any such MC sampling, the $g$ values we
generate are $not$ given by factual oracle $\mathscr{G}$. Rather they are
given by counter-factual oracles ${\mathscr{G}}'$.

To illustrate the foregoing, for simplicity assume that $D$
tells us that the oracle is noise-free. Then we can write
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {D}) \;\;=\; \;
{\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{G} \mid {D}) &=& \int
dG' \; P(G' \mid {D}) G'(x) \nonumber \\
&=& \int dG'dx \; T(G') H(x) \frac{P(G' \mid {D})
G'(x)}{T(G')H(x)} .
\end{eqnarray}
To estimate this integral using importance sampling, we generate $N_T$
samples of $T$ and $N_H$ samples of $H$. This gives us a set of $N_H
N_T$ values $G'(x)$. These are our fictitious samples. Our
 fictitious estimate of the integral is the average of those
values,
\begin{eqnarray}
{\tilde{\mathscr{F}}}_{P(G \mid {D})} &\equiv& \sum_{i=1}^{N_T} \sum_{j=1}^{N_H} \frac{G^i(x^j)} {N_T N_H
T(G^i)H(x^j)}.
\label{eq:fict_est}
\end{eqnarray}
(Obvious variants of this approach don't evaluate all $N_T$ oracles
$G^i$ at all $N_H$ points $x^j$.) 

***

Any such average is a high-dimensional integral. Moreover, typically
it cannot be evaluated closed form. An important exception
is that some Gaussian Process models with an appropriate covariance
matrix can be evaluated closed-form. See~ and references
therein. Sometimes one can use numerical expansions to approximate
the integral over $U$'s (or $G$'s, as the case may be). For example,
Laplace approximations can sometimes be used to do
this~ . In other cases though, it may make more sense to
use MC sampling.

***

Approximating the integral over $U$'s with such MC sampling introduces
a second process of MC, subsequent to the one that generated $D$.
That second MC process does $not$ involve calls to the actual oracle
$U$. Instead it samples the distribution $P(U \mid D)$ to generate
counter-factual $U$'s, and then samples those $U$'s. This gives us an
additional set of samples beyond the original samples that were
generated by calls to the true oracle. Intuitively speaking, we then
combine those two sets of samples, and optimize $\theta$ for the
resulting composite set.

We use the term ficticious estimation to refer to such
procedures, where one forms an estimate by combining an initial set of
samples of a `true' data-generation mechanism with other samples
that are generated subsequently to the original samples, and without
again invoking the true data-generation mechanism. We use the terms
 ficticious samples and ficticious sampling to refer to
that second set of samples and their generation, respectively. To
distinguish it from the ficticious samples, we call a $D$ that was
formed by importance sampling of the true oracle a set of factual
samples .

$ $

 ) Ficticious estimation for MCO 

$ $

***

To perform a statistical analysis of any type of MCO requires that
we first elaborate the statement that our `goal is to solve
(P2)'~ . We must specify exactly how happy we are
for any pair (the value of the random variable, the output of our
estimation algorithm). Formally, this is done with a function $L$
mapping the value of the variable whose value we do not know ,
together with the algorithm's output, to a real-valued `loss'. In
MCO, the `algorithm's output' is a value for $\phi$, and the
variable we do not know is $U$. So $L$ is a function of $U$ and
$\phi$.

***

As an example, say we have a function $G(x)$ that gives a `cost' for
$x$. Then under distribution $q_\theta(x)$, expected cost is $ dx
\; G(x) q_ (x)$. This is just the value of the loss of equation
Eq.~ , if we identify $w$ with $x$, $\phi$ with
$\theta$, and take $U(w, ) = U(x, ) = G(x)
q_ (x)$. Jumping ahead a bit, this expected cost is the
PC objective function ${\mathscr{F}}_G(q_\theta)$ of
Eq.~ below. Accordingly, we can interpret PC's
minimization of that ${\mathscr{F}}_G(q_\theta)$ as minimization of a
loss function given by expected value under $q_\theta$ of a cost
$G(x)$. 

***

In conventional MC, one forms an estimate of an integral by using
sample values of the integrand only. The associated sample locations
are not used. For example, consider importance-sampling MC estimation
of
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathscr{L}} &\equiv& \int dt \; f(t) \nonumber \\
&=& \int dt \; v(t) \frac{f(t)}{v(t)}
\end{eqnarray}
where $v$ is the proposal distribution. To form such an estimate one
generates $N$ IID samples of $v$, \ $t^i$\ , and evaluates the $N$
values $r^i \triangleq [f(t^i) / v(t^i)]$. One then estimates
${{\mathscr{L}}}$ using the maximum likelihood estimate,
\begin{eqnarray}
{{\mathscr{L}}} &\approx& \frac{\sum_i r^i}{N} \nonumber \\
&\equiv& {\tilde{{\mathscr{L}}}} .
\end{eqnarray}

***

sections.content:
Why should one do something like iterative focusing, or like setting
the objective to $pq$ distance for a sequence of $\beta$'s? If we do
follow an iterative procedure of this nature, how should we schedule
the changes to our objective?

To answer this, fix ${\mathscr{G}}$, and write the $qp$ distance from $q_\theta$
to the Boltzmann distribution at temperature $T$ as $qp_T(\theta)$.
Say our ultimate objective is to minimize ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. So $F(G,
q_ (x)) = G q_ (x)$, that is, $ E _ q_ (G) = qp$ distance
for $T = 0$. For simplicity, assume $G$ is nowhere negative, that
$h$ is uniform, and that $X$ is a compact subspace of a Euclidean
space, with non-zero measure.

Now one can form an IID sample of size $N$ from $h$, and then evaluate
the associated importance-sampling empirical estimate of
$qp_T(\theta)$ for every $\theta$. Label each of those estimates (one
for each $\theta$, $T$ being fixed to 0) by ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$.
For each $\theta$, as one forms independent size $N$ samples of $h$,
one induces a probability density function (pdf) over associated
values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. Call that set of pdf's (one for each
$\theta$) \ $\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$\ . Since $qp$ distance is
never negative, the support of each of those pdf's is the non-negative
ordinate values, that is, each pdf `starts' at the origin (if not at a
higher value).

In an idealized version of each iteration of immediate sampling with
$qp$ distance, we go through the following two-stage procedure:

$ $

 I) First we sample each pdf, getting associated
values (one for each $\theta$) \ ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$\ . 

$ $

 II) In the
second stage we choose the $\theta$ with the minimal
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. 

$ $

 Things are actually a bit more complicated,
since the samples are correlated, but ignore that for now. Also ignore
any quirks of getting caught in local minima in our EM algorithm (in
which case we don't end up minimizing ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over every
possible $\theta$), etc. Also, in general one needs some tie-breaking
scheme in (II). For now, ignore that as well.

Consider the pdf's in the subset of the \ $\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$\ 
corresponding to delta function $q_\theta$'s. For $T=0$, almost all of
these are candidates for the output of stage (II) of immediate
sampling. This is because for almost all delta-function $\theta$, for
our (fixed, finite) $N$ and uniform $h$, the pdf $\pi_\theta$ has
almost all of its mass at 0 for $T=0$. As a result, almost all
delta-function $\theta$ will result in ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$ ---
and we know that no $\theta$ can result in a lower
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$.

Now since importance samples are unbiased, each pdf
$\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_0)$ has as its mean the true $qp$ distance for
that $\theta$ and $T=0$. Write that true distance as
$qp_0(\theta)$. Since almost all the delta function pdf's have almost
all their mass at 0, the fact that their means are non-zero implies
that the widths of almost all delta function pdf's (that is, their
variances) must be gargantuan.

This means that at $T=0$, as one runs over the delta function
$q_\theta$'s, there will be horrible correlation between the associated
values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ (one for each $\theta$) and of
$qp_T(\theta)$. (Almost all such $\theta$ will result in
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$, but their values of $qp_T(\theta)$ will
vary considerably.) 

For tiny but non-zero $T$, there will be some variation in the values
of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ for the delta function $\theta$. Be we will
still have a horrible correlation. This lack of correlation between
what we minimize (${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$) and what we're interested in
($qp_T(\theta)$) means that we have no assurances that immediate
sampling will do what we want. Note that this problem is
almost absent in most parametric machine learning, being an artifact of how
weird $F$ is (from the point of view parametric machine learning). 

Currently, to address this problem we use a non-uniform $h$. To
choose that $h$ we start with a uniform $h$, and use non-zero
$T$. Having $T > 0$ means that each pdf is shifted rightward by $-T
S(q_ ) + ln (Z_T)$. The amount of shift varies from pdf
to pdf, with the delta function pdf's shifting by just ln$(Z_T)$. Note
that all other non-delta function pdf's are shifted rightward by less
than this. Accordingly, it is now possible that random samples of
those pdf's will be smaller values than random samples of the delta
function pdf's.

Due to this, the pdf's we will consider in stage (II) of immediate
sampling will change from what they were for $T=0$. Depending on $T$,
the pdf's that we consider will have relatively small variance (on the
scale of the difference between their means), especially in comparison
to the delta function pdf's. This means that there should be better
correlation (as one varies $\theta$) between the smallest
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values and the associated $qp(\theta)$ values
in the pdf's that we will consider.

We next use the $\theta$ minimizing ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ to set a new,
non-uniform $h$. Then we repeat, with some scheme or other for
shrinking $T$ as we do so. 

An alternative to this hack we currently use is to subtract a large
enough constant from $G$ so that it is nowhere positive (assuming such
a constant is finite). This means that every pdf now has support
restricted to $non-positive$ ordinate values (as compared to the
original scenario, where every pdf was restricted to positive values).

Note though that the delta function pdf's still have the same (huge)
density value at 0 as they did before. So samples
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ of those delta function pdf's are almost
guaranteed to give higher values than samples for the other (non-delta
function $\theta$) pdf's. This means that by searching for the
$\theta$'s with smaller ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$, we will $not$ be looking
at the delta function pdf's. Instead we will be looking at pdf's with
a far smaller variance. Those should have a relatively good
correlation between ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values and the associated
$qp(\theta)$ values. All without any need to set a parameter like $T$.

왜 반복적인 집중이나 $\beta$의 연속에 대해 목표를 $pq$ 거리로 설정해야 할까요? 이러한 성격의 반복 절차를 따르는 경우, 목표에 대한 변경 사항을 어떻게 계획해야 할까요?

이 질문에 답하기 위해 ${\mathscr{G}}$를 고정하고, 온도 $T$에서 볼츠만 분포까지의 $qp$ 거리를 $qp_T(\theta)$로 작성합니다. 우리의 궁극적인 목표는 ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$를 최소화하는 것입니다. 따라서 $F(G, q_ (x)) = G q_ (x)$, 즉 $E _ q_ (G) = qp$ 거리는 $T = 0$일 때입니다. 단순화를 위해 $G$는 어디서도 음수가 아니고, $h$는 균일하며, $X$는 비영(非零) 측도를 가진 유클리드 공간의 콤팩트 부분공간이라고 가정합니다.

이제 $h$에서 크기 $N$의 IID 샘플을 형성하고, 각 $\theta$에 대해 $qp_T(\theta)$의 관련 중요도 샘플링 경험적 추정치를 평가할 수 있습니다. 각 추정치를 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$로 레이블합니다(각 $\theta$에 대해, $T$는 0으로 고정됨). 각 $\theta$에 대해, $h$의 독립적인 크기 $N$ 샘플을 형성함에 따라, ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$의 관련 값에 대한 확률 밀도 함수(pdf)를 유도합니다. 그 pdf 집합을 $\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$라고 부릅니다. $qp$ 거리는 결코 음수가 아니므로, 각 pdf의 지지 집합은 비음수의 좌표 값입니다. 즉, 각 pdf는 원점에서 시작합니다(더 높은 값에서 시작하지 않는 경우).

$qp$ 거리로 즉각적인 샘플링의 각 반복의 이상화된 버전에서, 우리는 다음의 두 단계 절차를 거칩니다:

I) 먼저 각 pdf를 샘플링하여 관련 값(각 $\theta$에 대해 하나씩) ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$를 얻습니다.

II) 두 번째 단계에서 최소의 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$를 가진 $\theta$를 선택합니다.

사실 상황은 조금 더 복잡합니다. 샘플이 상관관계가 있기 때문입니다. 하지만 지금은 그 점을 무시하겠습니다. 또한 EM 알고리즘에서 지역 최소에 갇히는 것과 같은 특이점도 무시하겠습니다(이 경우 우리는 모든 가능한 $\theta$에 대해 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$를 최소화하지 못합니다). 일반적으로 (II)에서 어떤 동점 해소 방안이 필요합니다. 지금은 그것도 무시하겠습니다.

$\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$의 부분 집합에서 델타 함수 $q_\theta$에 해당하는 pdf를 고려해 보겠습니다. $T=0$일 때, 이러한 pdf의 거의 모든 것이 즉각적인 샘플링의 단계 (II)의 출력 후보입니다. 이는 거의 모든 델타 함수 $\theta$에 대해, 고정된 유한한 $N$과 균일한 $h$에 대해, pdf $\pi_\theta$가 $T=0$일 때 거의 모든 질량을 0에 두기 때문입니다. 결과적으로, 거의 모든 델타 함수 $\theta$는 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$이 되고 --- 우리는 어떤 $\theta$도 더 낮은 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$를 가질 수 없다는 것을 알고 있습니다.

이제 중요도 샘플이 편향되지 않기 때문에, 각 pdf $\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_0)$의 평균은 해당 $\theta$와 $T=0$에 대한 진정한 $qp$ 거리입니다. 그 진정한 거리를 $qp_0(\theta)$로 작성합니다. 거의 모든 델타 함수 pdf가 거의 모든 질량을 0에 두기 때문에, 그 평균이 0이 아님을 의미하는 것은 거의 모든 델타 함수 pdf의 폭(즉, 분산)이 거대해야 한다는 것을 의미합니다.

이는 $T=0$일 때 델타 함수 $q_\theta$를 통해 실행할 경우, ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$(각 $\theta$에 대해 하나씩)와 $qp_T(\theta)$의 관련 값 간에 끔찍한 상관관계가 있을 것임을 의미합니다. (거의 모든 그러한 $\theta$는 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$이지만, 그들의 $qp_T(\theta)$ 값은 상당히 다를 것입니다.)

작지만 0이 아닌 $T$에 대해, 델타 함수 $\theta$에 대한 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ 값에 약간의 변동이 있을 것입니다. 그러나 여전히 끔찍한 상관관계가 있을 것입니다. 우리가 최소화하는 것(${ \hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$)과 우리가 관심 있는 것($qp_T(\theta)$) 간의 이러한 상관관계 부족은 즉각적인 샘플링이 우리가 원하는 대로 작동할 것이라는 보장이 없음을 의미합니다. 이 문제는 대부분의 파라메트릭 머신 러닝에서는 거의 발생하지 않으며, 이는 파라메트릭 머신 러닝의 관점에서 $F$가 얼마나 이상한지의 산물입니다.

현재 이 문제를 해결하기 위해 우리는 비균일한 $h$를 사용합니다. 그 $h$를 선택하기 위해 우리는 균일한 $h$로 시작하고 비영(非零) $T$를 사용합니다. $T > 0$이면 각 pdf는 $-T S(q_ ) + \ln (Z_T)$만큼 오른쪽으로 이동합니다. 이동량은 pdf마다 다르며, 델타 함수 pdf는 단지 $\ln(Z_T)$만큼 이동합니다. 다른 비델타 함수 pdf는 이보다 덜 오른쪽으로 이동합니다. 따라서 이제 이러한 pdf의 무작위 샘플이 델타 함수 pdf의 무작위 샘플보다 작은 값을 가질 가능성이 있습니다.

이로 인해 즉각적인 샘플링의 단계 (II)에서 고려할 pdf는 $T=0$일 때의 것과 달라질 것입니다. $T$에 따라 우리가 고려하는 pdf는 상대적으로 작은 분산을 가질 것이며(그들의 평균 간의 차이의 척도에서), 특히 델타 함수 pdf와 비교할 때 더욱 그렇습니다. 이는 우리가 고려할 pdf에서 가장 작은 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ 값과 관련된 $qp(\theta)$ 값 간에 더 나은 상관관계가 있어야 함을 의미합니다.

다음으로 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$를 최소화하는 $\theta$를 사용하여 새로운 비균일한 $h$를 설정합니다. 그런 다음 우리는 그렇게 하면서 $T$를 줄이기 위한 어떤 방식으로 반복합니다.

현재 우리가 사용하는 이 해킹의 대안은 $G$에서 충분히 큰 상수를 빼서 어디서도 양수가 되지 않도록 하는 것입니다(그런 상수가 유한하다고 가정할 때). 이는 이제 모든 pdf가 비양수의 좌표 값으로 제한된 지지를 가지게 됨을 의미합니다(원래 시나리오에서는 모든 pdf가 양수 값으로 제한되었습니다).

그러나 델타 함수 pdf는 여전히 이전과 동일한(거대한) 밀도 값을 0에서 가지고 있다는 점에 유의하십시오. 따라서 이러한 델타 함수 pdf의 샘플 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$는 다른(비델타 함수 $\theta$) pdf의 샘플보다 높은 값을 제공할 가능성이 거의 보장됩니다. 이는 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$가 더 작은 $\theta$를 찾는 과정에서 델타 함수 pdf를 보지 않게 됨을 의미합니다. 대신 우리는 훨씬 작은 분산을 가진 pdf를 보게 될 것입니다. 이러한 pdf는 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ 값과 관련된 $qp(\theta)$ 값 간에 상대적으로 좋은 상관관계를 가져야 합니다. 모든 것이 $T$와 같은 매개변수를 설정할 필요 없이 이루어집니다.

summary.content: 이 섹션에서는 반복적인 초점 맞추기와 목표를 설정하는 방법에 대해 논의하고 있습니다. 저자는 Boltzmann 분포와의 $qp$ 거리인 $qp_T(\theta)$를 최소화하는 것이 궁극적인 목표라고 설명하며, 이를 위해 IID 샘플을 사용하여 각 $\theta$에 대한 중요도 샘플링 추정치를 평가합니다. $T=0$에서의 delta 함수 pdf는 대부분의 질량이 0에 집중되어 있어, 샘플링 과정에서 상관관계가 심각하게 발생한다고 지적합니다. 이를 해결하기 위해 비균일한 $h$를 사용하고, $T$를 증가시켜 pdf의 분산을 줄임으로써 더 나은 상관관계를 얻는 방법을 제안합니다.

sections.content:
A variant of the procedure we use now exploits cross-validation to set
$T$. To motivate this variant, note that our problem is that even
though ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ is an unbiased estimate of
$qp_T(\theta)$, it's variance for $T=0$ is so large that we can't use
its value as a guide to set $\theta$. As we go from one $\theta$ to
another, $qp_T(\theta)$ may change in ways completely at odds with how
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ changes, leading us badly astray in setting
$\theta$.

Everything else being equal, we want to search for $\theta$'s that
minimize ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over a set ${\mathscr{Q}}$ of
$\theta$'s that have good correlation between ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$
and $qp_T(\theta)$ (again, where `correlation' is as one varies
over ${\mathscr{Q}}$). More precisely, for any $T$, we want such a good
correlation over a set $U_T$ of $\theta$'s that have small associated
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values, those being the $\theta$'s that our
descent procedure will focus on. (The end of our procedure for
implementing stage II of immediate sampling will, indirectly or
otherwise, be a search over such a set $U_T$.)

To formalize this, first recall that the expectation over sample sets $d$ of
${\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) =  qp_{T}(\theta)$, since we're using an
unbiased estimator, ${\hat{qp}}$. Let $P(\theta)$ be some distribution 
(e.g., uniform) over (the $\theta$ in) $U_T$. Define 
\begin{eqnarray}
{\hat{qp}}_{T,d} &\triangleq& \int d \theta \; P(\theta)
{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta).
\end{eqnarray}
Now consider the covariance
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}_d  \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  
\times [qp_{T}(\theta) - qp_T] \}
\end{eqnarray}
where $qp_T \equiv \int d \theta \; P(\theta) qp_{T}(\theta)$. This
expectation is how well on average (over sample sets $d$), what we
actually search on (values of ${\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta)$ for $\theta$
chosen from $U_T$) covaries with what we're interested in (values of
$qp_{T}(\theta)$).

Since our estimator is unbiased, this expected covariance is just the
variance of $qp_T(\theta)$ under $P(\theta)$. However for our
purposes, we want to use unbiasedness differently, to expand the
expected covariance as:
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}_d \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  
\times [ {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}]] \}.
\end{eqnarray}
This in turn just equals
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  
\times [ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}] \}.
\label{eq:cov}
\end{eqnarray}

More carefully, it isn't the expected covariance we're interested in, but rather
the associated expected correlation,
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}_d  \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [ \frac{ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) -
{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}} { \sqrt{ {\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]}}
\times \frac{qp_{T}(\theta) - qp_T} { \sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]}} ] \}
\end{eqnarray}
where the two denominator variances in the integrand are defined in
the obvious way, in terms the associated numerators. As before, we can
use the unbiasedness of our estimator to expand this expected
correlation, getting
\begin{eqnarray}
{\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta)
[\frac{{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}}{
\sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}] }}
\times \frac{ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}} { \sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]}}] \}.
\label{eq:corr}
\end{eqnarray}
Note that the two denominator variances are different. As a crude
approximation, one could just assume that Var$[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]$ does
not change much as one varies $d$. In that case, up to the overall
multiplicative factor $[{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]]^{-1}$, we can
approximate Eq.~ with
\begin{eqnarray}
 {\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) 
     [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}] \times
     [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}] \}.
\label{eq:corr_approx}
\end{eqnarray}

We want the correlation of Eq.~ to be as high as possible,
that is, we want to know what $T$ will cause that. So in the usual
bootstrap way, for any given $T$ and sample set $d$, we can subsample
$d$, and use those subsamples to estimate the expression in
Eq.~ (or Eq.~ ). For any fixed $d$, we
can estimate the correlation this way for many different $T$'s. We can
then choose the $T$ that maximizes those subsample-based estimates of
the expression in Eq.~ . That $T$ is the one we would use
to set the Boltzmann distribution $p_T$ in our $qp$ distance.

As a crude example of this scheme, for each $\theta \in U_T$, we
measure two values. The first is the value of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$
on a `held-in' subset of our sample (of $x$'s generated by IID
sampling $h$). The second is the value of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ on
the held-out remainder of our sample. We then measure the correlation,
across all the $\theta$'s in $U_T$, between the values of
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ in the held-in samples and the values in the
held-out samples.

To see why this makes sense, note that for $T=0$, $U_T$ will almost
definitely consist of delta function $q_\theta$'s. So the correlation
between the values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ in the held-in samples
and the values in the held-out samples will be zero. For $T
 $, the $q_ U_T $ will all be close to uniform. I
$suspect$ the correlation will again be small. For a sweet spot
between these regimes, the correlation will be maximized.

A probably preferable modification of this procedure replaces
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ as the value from the held-out sample with the
empirical average $G$ as the value from the held-out sample (that is, it
replaces it with `${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$' for zero $T$). In this
variant one would find the $T$ that has a high correlation (over
$\theta \in U_T$) between those empirical estimates of expected $G$
and the ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values on the held-in points. The
reasoning is that it is ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$ that we're ultimately
interested in, and properly speaking, Eq.~ should be
modified accordingly.

Consider the `sweet spot' $T$ for this correlation between held-in
sample values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ and held-out sample values of
${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. It is at this $T$ that minimizing
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over all $U_T$ --- our immediate sampling
procedure --- has the highest probability of minimizing (an unbiased
estimate of) ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta \in U_T}(G)$.

As a practical matter, we may not want to just search for the $T$ that
maximizes this correlation of the elements in the associated
$U_T$. After all, one can imagine a situation where that correlation
is high, but the associated (held-out sample estimate of)
${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$ is poor. In such a case, for our best-correlating
$T$, the ordering of the values ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ accurately tracks
the ordering of associated values of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. However
finding the $q_\theta \in U_T$ that minimizes ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$
will not (likely) result in a good value of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. The
problem is that while the correlation is high, $U_T$ consists only of
poor $q_\theta$. So being able to reliably choose the best element of
that $U_T$ isn't very helpful.

As one way around this, for each $T$, form a regression. The
independent variable in this regression is the held-in sample values
of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. The dependent variable is the associated
held-out sample values of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. The `training set' for
this regression is formed from the $\theta \in U_T$. 

Write this regression as the function $w(v)$ taking $ R 
 R $. Write the associated ($v$-varying) error
bar of the regression as $\sigma(v)$. Finally, for any $T$, let
${\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T)$ be the $\theta \in U_T$ that minimizes
${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ (that is, that minimizes the independent variable
of our regression) over the entire sample. Then it may make sense to
use the $T$ that (to be conservative) minimizes
$w({\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T)) + \sigma({\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T))$. This is
our estimate of what an `unlucky' value of
${\mathbb{E}}_{q_{\hat{opt}}(T)}(G)$ would be, for using immediate
sampling to pick a $\theta \in U_T$. In other words, it's our estimate
of what ${\mathbb{E}}_q(G)$ would for an unlucky run of immediate sampling.

There are obvious variants of all of this for $pq$ distance, etc.

summary.content: 이 섹션에서는 크로스 검증을 활용하여 최적의 온도 $T$를 설정하는 방법을 제안합니다. ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$가 $qp_T(\theta)$의 불편 추정량임에도 불구하고, $T=0$에서의 분산이 커서 $\theta$ 설정에 어려움이 발생합니다. 따라서, ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$와 $qp_T(\theta)$ 간의 상관관계를 최대화하는 $\theta$를 찾기 위해, 여러 샘플 세트를 사용하여 상관관계를 추정하고 최적의 $T$를 선택합니다. 이 과정에서, 최적의 $T$는 ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$의 최소화를 통해 ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$의 추정치를 개선하는 데 기여합니다.

It is worth considering the conventional use of cross-validation to
set a regularization parameter in parametertic parametric machine learning in
light of the foregoing. Simplify such cross-validation into the
following procedure:

$ $

 A) Form an $N$-element training set, $d_1$, by IID sampling
$P(x) P(y \mid x)$, and find the $\theta$ that minimizes the
associated value
\begin{eqnarray}
{\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i
L^i_1(\theta) + T R(\theta)}{N}
\end{eqnarray}
where $T$ is the regularization parameter, $R$ is the regularizer, and
the $L^i_1(\theta)$ are the $N$ functions from $\theta$ to
${\mathbb{R}}$ induced by evaluating $L(y, z_\theta(x))$ at the $x-y$
pairs in $D_1$. For use below, define $\theta(D_1, T)$ as that
minimizing $\theta$. (This quantity is the parametric machine learning
analogue of the quantity ${\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T))$ discussed above.)

$ $ 

 B) Form an $N$-element training set, $d_2$, by IID sampling
$P(x) P(y \mid x)$. Evaluate
\begin{eqnarray}
{\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i
L^i_1(\theta)}{N}
\end{eqnarray}
for $\theta = \theta(D_1, T)$.
$ $

${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$ is an unbiased estimate of the
value of the integral in Eq.~ evaluated for $ 
= (D_1, T)$. We do steps (A, B) for a set of several $T$, and
then find the $T$ that minimizes $ Gen-Err ( (D_1,
T))$. Our final fit is given by $z_ (D_1, T) $ for that $T$.

In light of our discussion on correlation in the preceding section, it
is clear that there is a danger with this simplified version of
cross-validation. While the estimates of the integral in
Eq.~ given by $ Gen-Err ( (D_1,
T))$ are all unbiased, they may have high variances. In such a
scenario, using the $T$ that minimizes $ Gen-Err 
( (D_1, T))$ may give poor results.

To get around this, one might want to restrict attention to $T$ for
which the associated variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$
is small. The problem is that it may be difficult even to ascertain
whether the variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$ is
small; one might not even know that one has a problem. 

One way to address that is to assume that the variance of
${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ is a slowly varying function of
${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$. That way we can look at many
$\theta$ such that ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$ is close to
${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T)$ and see how much
${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ `bounces around' across those
neighboring $\theta$. This is what the idea of using a regression
$w(v)$, recounted in the previous section, tries to do; $v$ is
${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$, and $w$ is $ Gen-Err 
( )$.

Indeed, even if the variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ is
fairly constant across the $T$ we're considering, it may make sense to
use such a regression to estimate what $T$ would result in an optimal
choice of $\theta(D_1, T)$. To see this, define $v^* 
 Tr-Err ( (D_1, T))$, and $w^* 
 Gen-Err ( (D_1, T))$. Then intuitively, with
regression, for each $T$ one uses curve-fitting to combine the pair
$(v^*, w^*)$ with neighboring $(v, w)$ pairs. That combination
provides one's estimate of the full error integral for $v^*$, that is,
for $\theta(D_1, T)$. In contrast, in conventional cross-validation,
one ignores the information in those neighboring $v$'s, and just uses
the value $w^*$ as one's estimate of the full error integral for
$\theta(D_1, T)$.

***

To that end, first note that the oracle is noise-free. This means that
the posterior $P({G_c} \mid {{D}})$ only allows ${G_c}$'s that, if
sampled at the $x$'s in ${{D}}$, would produce the associated
$G(x)$ values found in ${{D}}$. In other words, if the
fictitious sampling of $H$ produced the $x$'s in ${D}$, then
the associated fictitious sampling of $T$ would have to result in the
factual sample values $G(x)$ found in ${D}$.

This suggests that the factual samples are in some sense consistent
with fictitious sampling. To formalize this one might consider whether
${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an unbiased estimate of the
Bayesian integral ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$.
If it is, a natural idea for how to form our final estimate would be
to use a weighted average of the fictitious and factual estimates,
with the weights set using a bias-variance approach.

One must be careful however. Strictly speaking there is no sense in
which one can even ask if ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an
unbiased estimate of $ E ( F _ G_c 
 D )$, since that expectation value is only defined once
${D}$ is fixed. Similarly, there are two variances we can
consider. One is a composite variance one could construct based on the
point-variances Var$({G_c}(x^i_c) \mid {{D}})$, that is, based on the
posterior variances of ${G_c}$ at the fictitious sample points. Another
is the variance of ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$
(as one varies ${D}$) as an estimator of
${\mathscr{F}}_G$. However these two variances have no direct relation
to one another; they concern different underlying stochastic
processes.

As an alternative, one could ask what the relative weights of
${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ and $ F _ P( G_c 
 D ) $ should be when both are viewed as estimators of
$\int dx \; G(x)$. In doing this one would consider how the outputs of
those two estimators of $\int dx \; G(x)$ behave as one varies
${D}$ from one (factual) importance sample to another.

${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an unbiased estimator of
$\int dx \; G(x)$. Its variance is trivial to estimate. To estimate
the variance of ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$, we
could use the bootstrap. That would entail generating random subsets
of ${{D}}$ with replacement, and then forming fictitious
estimates of $\int dx \; G(x)$ for each of those subsets. 

Estimating the bias of $ F _ P( G_c 
 D ) $ is more problematic. The simplest approach would be
to treat that bias as though it were the difference between
${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$ and
${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$, for the purposes of calculating
the averaging weights. However recall that in general the bias of
Bayesian estimates is nonzero. So using a weighting of the two
estimates based on bias-variance considerations, even in the limit of
an infinite number of fictitious samples, where the fictitious
estimate ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$ exacty
equals ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$, one would
not use that FB estimate by itself. Rather one would average
if with the factual estimate. This disagrees with the prescription of
Bayesian decision theory.

***

N.b., the GA-like view of the results of using xvalidation to
dynamically adapt the number of mixing components: you're adding and
removing species, as needed to speed the optimization.

***
 DHW, DEV: This section must ge fixed up. Shorten it to just have
a copy of the abstract, and then a quick mention of other kinds of PL
techniques we can test. 

One obvious way to apply PL techniques to blackbox optimization is to
exploit parametric supervised learning to form a `fit'
${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$ to the samples of the oracle. One then searches
for the minimum of ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$. This allows the optimization
to proceed with relatively few calls to the actual oracle. This
approach is essentially what is done in Response Surface Methods
(RSM)~ .

Note that this approach provides us with a new optimization problem
over the same space $X$ as the original blackbox optimization
problem. That new problem is in addition to the PL problem of finding
$\theta$ from the samples. So this approach provides us with a
succession of two search problems. Note also that this approach
involves only a specific PL technique, namely the one used to do the
supervised learning.

In contrast, in this paper we do not consider how to apply some
specific PL technique to design a new blackbox optimization algorithm.
Rather we start with the blackbox optimization algorithm of immediate
sampling. We establish that the search underlying immediate sampling
is mathematically identical to the search underlying PL in its
broadest sense. This identity reduces immediate sampling and its
serach process in toto to PL and its search process. So to
apply PL to blackbox optimization there is no need to add a subsequent
search to the search of PL, e.g., a search over the fit
${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$. The search of PL suffices.

전통적인 교차 검증을 사용하여 매개변수 기계 학습에서 정규화 매개변수를 설정하는 것에 대해 앞서 논의한 내용을 고려할 가치가 있다. 이러한 교차 검증을 다음 절차로 단순화하자:

$ $

A) IID 샘플링 $P(x) P(y \mid x)$을 통해 $N$ 요소의 훈련 세트 $d_1$을 형성하고, 다음과 같은 연관된 값을 최소화하는 $\theta$를 찾는다.
\begin{eqnarray}
{\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i L^i_1(\theta) + T R(\theta)}{N}
\end{eqnarray}
여기서 $T$는 정규화 매개변수, $R$은 정규화 함수이며, $L^i_1(\theta)$는 $D_1$의 $x-y$ 쌍에서 $L(y, z_\theta(x))$를 평가하여 유도된 $\theta$에서의 $N$ 함수이다. 아래에서 사용할 수 있도록, $\theta(D_1, T)$를 $\theta$를 최소화하는 것으로 정의한다. (이 양은 위에서 논의한 ${\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T)$의 매개변수 기계 학습 유사체이다.)

$ $

B) IID 샘플링 $P(x) P(y \mid x)$을 통해 $N$ 요소의 훈련 세트 $d_2$를 형성한다. $\theta = \theta(D_1, T)$에 대해 다음을 평가한다.
\begin{eqnarray}
{\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i L^i_1(\theta)}{N}
\end{eqnarray}
$ $

${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$는 $= (D_1, T)$에 대해 평가된 적분의 값에 대한 편향 없는 추정치이다. 우리는 여러 $T$에 대해 (A, B) 단계를 수행한 후, $Gen-Err((D_1, T))$를 최소화하는 $T$를 찾는다. 우리의 최종 적합은 해당 $T$에 대해 $z(D_1, T)$로 주어진다.

앞서 섹션에서의 상관관계에 대한 논의를 고려할 때, 이 단순화된 교차 검증 버전에는 위험이 있다는 것이 분명하다. $Gen-Err((D_1, T))$에 의해 주어진 적분의 추정치는 모두 편향이 없지만, 높은 분산을 가질 수 있다. 이러한 시나리오에서는 $Gen-Err((D_1, T))$를 최소화하는 $T$를 사용하는 것이 좋지 않은 결과를 초래할 수 있다.

이를 해결하기 위해, ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$의 관련 분산이 작은 $T$에 주의를 제한하고자 할 수 있다. 문제는 ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$의 분산이 작은지 확인하는 것이 어려울 수 있다는 점이다; 문제를 가지고 있다는 사실조차 알지 못할 수 있다.

이를 해결하는 한 가지 방법은 ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$의 분산이 ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$의 느리게 변하는 함수라고 가정하는 것이다. 그렇게 하면 ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$가 ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$에 가까운 많은 $\theta$를 살펴보고, 그 이웃 $\theta$들 사이에서 ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$가 얼마나 '튀는지' 볼 수 있다. 이것이 이전 섹션에서 언급한 회귀 $w(v)$를 사용하는 아이디어가 시도하는 것이다; $v$는 ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$이고, $w$는 $Gen-Err()$이다.

실제로, ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$의 분산이 우리가 고려하는 $T$ 전반에 걸쳐 상당히 일정하더라도, 그러한 회귀를 사용하여 최적의 $\theta(D_1, T)$를 초래할 $T$를 추정하는 것이 의미가 있을 수 있다. 이를 보기 위해, $v^* Tr-Err((D_1, T))$와 $w^* Gen-Err((D_1, T))$를 정의하자. 그러면 직관적으로 회귀를 통해 각 $T$에 대해 곡선 맞춤을 사용하여 쌍 $(v^*, w^*)$를 이웃 $(v, w)$ 쌍과 결합한다. 그 결합은 $v^*$, 즉 $\theta(D_1, T)$에 대한 전체 오류 적분의 추정치를 제공한다. 대조적으로, 전통적인 교차 검증에서는 이러한 이웃 $v$의 정보를 무시하고, 단순히 $w^*$ 값을 $\theta(D_1, T)$에 대한 전체 오류 적분의 추정치로 사용한다.

***

이를 위해, 먼저 오라클이 노이즈가 없다는 점에 주목하자. 이는 사후 확률 $P({G_c} \mid {{D}})$가 ${D}$의 $x$에서 샘플링될 경우 연관된 $G(x)$ 값을 생성할 수 있는 ${G_c}$만 허용한다는 것을 의미한다. 즉, 허구의 샘플링 $H$가 ${D}$의 $x$를 생성했다면, 연관된 허구의 샘플링 $T$는 ${D}$에서 발견된 사실적 샘플 값 $G(x)$를 생성해야 한다.

이는 사실적 샘플이 어떤 의미에서 허구의 샘플링과 일관성이 있음을 시사한다. 이를 형식화하기 위해, ${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_{{D}}$가 베이지안 적분 ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$의 편향 없는 추정치인지 여부를 고려할 수 있다. 만약 그렇다면, 최종 추정치를 형성하는 자연스러운 아이디어는 편향-분산 접근을 사용하여 허구의 추정치와 사실적 추정치의 가중 평균을 사용하는 것이다.

그러나 주의해야 한다. 엄밀히 말하면, ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$가 $E(F_G D)$의 편향 없는 추정치인지 물어볼 수 있는 의미는 없다. 왜냐하면 그 기대값은 ${D}$가 고정된 후에만 정의되기 때문이다. 마찬가지로, 우리가 고려할 수 있는 두 가지 분산이 있다. 하나는 점 분산 Var$({G_c}(x^i_c) \mid {{D}})$를 기반으로 구성할 수 있는 복합 분산이며, 이는 허구의 샘플 포인트에서 ${G_c}$의 사후 분산에 기반한다. 다른 하나는 ${\mathscr{F}}_G$의 추정치로서 ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$의 분산이다 (이때 ${D}$를 변화시킨다). 그러나 이 두 분산은 서로 직접적인 관계가 없다; 서로 다른 기본 확률 과정에 관한 것이다.

대안으로, ${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_{{D}}$와 $F_P(G_c D)$가 $\int dx \; G(x)$의 추정치로 볼 때 상대적인 가중치가 무엇이어야 하는지를 물을 수 있다. 이를 수행할 때, 두 추정치의 출력이 ${D}$를 하나의 (사실적) 중요 샘플에서 다른 것으로 변화시킬 때 어떻게 행동하는지를 고려할 것이다.

${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_{{D}}$는 $\int dx \; G(x)$의 편향 없는 추정치이다. 그 분산은 추정하기가 간단하다. ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$의 분산을 추정하기 위해 부트스트랩을 사용할 수 있다. 이는 대체로 ${D}$의 무작위 하위 집합을 생성하고, 각 하위 집합에 대해 $\int dx \; G(x)$의 허구의 추정치를 형성하는 것을 포함한다.

$F_P(G_c D)$의 편향을 추정하는 것은 더 문제가 된다. 가장 간단한 접근법은 그 편향을 ${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_D(\theta)$와 ${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_{{D}}$의 차이로 취급하여 평균 가중치를 계산하는 것이다. 그러나 일반적으로 베이지안 추정치의 편향은 0이 아님을 기억하라. 따라서 편향-분산 고려에 따라 두 추정치의 가중치를 사용하는 것은, 허구의 샘플 수가 무한대에 가까워져서 허구의 추정치 ${\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}_D(\theta)$가 ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$와 정확히 같아지는 경우에도, 그 FB 추정치를 단독으로 사용하지 않을 것이다. 오히려 사실적 추정치와 평균을 내야 한다. 이는 베이지안 의사결정 이론의 처방과 일치하지 않는다.

***

참고로, xvalidation을 사용하여 혼합 성분의 수를 동적으로 조정하는 결과에 대한 GA와 유사한 관점: 최적화를 가속화하기 위해 종을 추가하고 제거하고 있다.

***
DHW, DEV: 이 섹션은 수정되어야 한다. 초록의 복사본만 포함하고, 우리가 테스트할 수 있는 다른 종류의 PL 기술에 대한 간단한 언급을 추가하라.

PL 기술을 블랙박스 최적화에 적용하는 명백한 방법 중 하나는 매개변수 감독 학습을 활용하여 오라클의 샘플에 대한 '적합' ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$을 형성하는 것이다. 그런 다음 ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$의 최소값을 찾는다. 이는 실제 오라클에 대한 호출을 상대적으로 적게 하면서 최적화를 진행할 수 있게 한다. 이 접근법은 응답 표면 방법(Response Surface Methods, RSM)에서 수행되는 기본적인 방법이다.

이 접근법은 원래 블랙박스 최적화 문제와 동일한 공간 $X$에 대한 새로운 최적화 문제를 제공한다. 그 새로운 문제는 샘플에서 $\theta$를 찾는 PL 문제 외에도 존재한다. 따라서 이 접근법은 두 개의 검색 문제의 연속을 제공한다. 또한 이 접근법은 특정 PL 기술, 즉 감독 학습을 수행하는 데 사용되는 기술만 포함한다.

대조적으로, 이 논문에서는 특정 PL 기술을 적용하여 새로운 블랙박스 최적화 알고리즘을 설계하는 방법을 고려하지 않는다. 오히려 우리는 즉각적인 샘플링의 블랙박스 최적화 알고리즘에서 시작한다. 우리는 즉각적인 샘플링의 기초가 PL의 가장 넓은 의미에서의 기초와 수학적으로 동일하다는 것을 확립한다. 이 동일성은 즉각적인 샘플링과 그 검색 과정을 PL과 그 검색 과정으로 완전히 축소한다. 따라서 PL을 블랙박스 최적화에 적용하기 위해 PL의 검색에 후속 검색을 추가할 필요가 없다. 즉, ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$에 대한 검색이 필요하지 않다. PL의 검색만으로 충분하다.

summary.content: 전통적인 교차 검증을 통해 파라메트릭 기계 학습에서 정규화 매개변수를 설정하는 방법을 간소화하여 설명하였다. 이 과정에서 두 개의 훈련 세트를 형성하고, 각각의 세트에 대해 트레이닝 오류와 일반화 오류를 평가하여 최적의 정규화 매개변수를 찾는다. 그러나 이러한 방법은 일반화 오류의 추정치가 높은 분산을 가질 수 있어, 최적의 결과를 보장하지 못할 위험이 있다. 이를 해결하기 위해, 인접한 매개변수들에 대한 일반화 오류의 변동성을 분석하고 회귀 분석을 통해 최적의 매개변수를 추정하는 방법을 제안하였다.

paper.title: Calculating Valid Domains for BDD-Based Interactive Configuration
paper.title_ko: BDD 기반 상호작용 구성의 유효 도메인 계산
paper.author: Tarik Hadzic, Rune Moller Jensen, Henrik Reif Andersen

sections.content:
In these notes we formally describe the functionality of
Calculating Valid Domains from the BDD representing the solution
space of valid configurations. The formalization is largely based
on the CLab configuration framework.
sections.content_ko: 이 노트에서는 유효한 구성의 솔루션 공간을 나타내는 BDD에서 유효한 도메인을 계산하는 기능을 공식적으로 설명합니다. 이 공식화는 주로 CLab 구성 프레임워크를 기반으로 합니다.

summary.content: 이 논문에서는 유효한 구성의 솔루션 공간을 나타내는 BDD에서 유효한 도메인을 계산하는 기능을 공식적으로 설명합니다. 이 공식화는 주로 CLab 구성 프레임워크를 기반으로 하고 있습니다.

sections.content:
Interactive configuration problems are special applications of
Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP) where a user is assisted in
interactively assigning values to variables by a software tool.
This software, called a configurator, assists the user by
calculating and displaying the available, valid choices for each
unassigned variable in what are called valid domains
computations. Application areas include customising physical
products (such as PC's and cars) and services (such as airplane
tickets and insurances).

Three important features are required of a tool that implements
interactive configuration: it should be complete (all valid
configurations should be reachable through user interaction),
backtrack-free (a user is never forced to change an earlier choice
due to incompleteness in the logical deductions), and it should
provide real-time performance (feedback should be fast enough to
allow real-time interactions). The requirement of obtaining
backtrack-freeness while maintaining completeness makes the
problem of calculating valid domains NP-hard. The real-time
performance requirement enforces further that runtime calculations
are bounded in polynomial time. According to user-interface
design criteria, for a user to perceive interaction as being
real-time, system response needs to be within about 250
milliseconds in practice . Therefore,
the current approaches that meet all three conditions use off-line
precomputation to generate an efficient runtime data structure
representing the solution space .
The challenge with this data structure is that the solution space
is almost always exponentially large and it is NP-hard to find.
Despite the bad worst-case bounds, it has nevertheless turned out
in real industrial applications that the data structures can often
be kept small .
sections.content_ko:
인터랙티브 구성 문제는 사용자가 소프트웨어 도구에 의해 변수에 값을 대화형으로 할당하는 데 도움을 받는 제약 만족 문제(Constraint Satisfaction Problems, CSP)의 특별한 응용입니다. 이 소프트웨어는 구성기(configurator)라고 하며, 사용자가 할당되지 않은 각 변수에 대한 사용 가능한 유효 선택을 계산하고 표시함으로써 사용자를 지원합니다. 이러한 계산을 유효 도메인(valid domains) 계산이라고 합니다. 응용 분야에는 물리적 제품(예: PC 및 자동차)과 서비스(예: 항공권 및 보험)의 맞춤화가 포함됩니다.

인터랙티브 구성을 구현하는 도구에는 세 가지 중요한 기능이 필요합니다: 완전성(모든 유효 구성은 사용자 상호작용을 통해 도달 가능해야 함), 백트랙 프리(backtrack-free)성(사용자는 논리적 추론의 불완전성으로 인해 이전 선택을 변경하도록 강요받지 않아야 함), 그리고 실시간 성능(real-time performance)을 제공해야 합니다(피드백은 실시간 상호작용을 허용할 만큼 빠르게 이루어져야 함). 완전성을 유지하면서 백트랙 프리성을 얻는 요구는 유효 도메인을 계산하는 문제를 NP-난해(NP-hard)하게 만듭니다. 실시간 성능 요구는 런타임 계산이 다항 시간(polynomial time)으로 제한되어야 한다는 추가적인 제약을 부과합니다. 사용자 인터페이스 설계 기준에 따르면, 사용자가 상호작용을 실시간으로 인식하기 위해서는 시스템 응답이 실제로 약 250밀리초 이내에 이루어져야 합니다. 따라서, 세 가지 조건을 모두 충족하는 현재의 접근 방식은 효율적인 런타임 데이터 구조를 생성하기 위해 오프라인 사전 계산(off-line precomputation)을 사용합니다. 

이 데이터 구조의 도전 과제는 솔루션 공간이 거의 항상 지수적으로 크며, 이를 찾는 것이 NP-난해하다는 것입니다. 최악의 경우 경계가 나쁘지만, 실제 산업 응용에서는 이러한 데이터 구조를 종종 작게 유지할 수 있다는 것이 밝혀졌습니다.

summary.content: 인터랙티브 구성 문제는 사용자가 소프트웨어 도구의 도움을 받아 변수에 값을 할당하는 제약 만족 문제의 특수한 응용입니다. 이러한 도구는 유효한 도메인 계산을 통해 각 할당되지 않은 변수에 대한 유효한 선택지를 계산하고 표시합니다. 이 도구는 완전성, 백트래킹이 없고, 실시간 성능을 제공해야 하며, 유효한 도메인을 계산하는 문제는 NP-하드입니다. 현재의 접근 방식은 오프라인 사전 계산을 통해 효율적인 런타임 데이터 구조를 생성하여 이 세 가지 조건을 충족시키고 있으며, 실제 산업 응용에서는 이 데이터 구조를 작게 유지할 수 있는 경우가 많습니다.

sections.content:
The input model to an interactive configuration problem is
 a special kind of Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP)
 where constraints are represented as
propositional formulas:

 definition 
A configuration model $C$ is a triple $(X,D,F)$ where X is
a set of variables $\{x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1}\}$, $D = D_0 
 D_ n-1 $ is the Cartesian product of their finite
domains $D_0, \ldots ,D_{n-1}$ and $F = \{f_0, . . . , f_{m-1}\}$
is a set of propositional formulae over atomic propositions $x_i =
v$, where $v D_i$, specifying conditions on the values of the
variables.
 definition 

Concretely, every domain can be defined as $D_i = \ 0, ,
|D_i|-1 \ $. An assignment of values $v_0, , v_ n-1 $ to
variables $x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ is denoted as an assignment $ 
= \ (x_0,v_0), ,(x_ n-1 ,v_ n-1 )\ $. Domain of assignment
$dom(\rho)$ is the set of variables which are assigned: $dom( )
= \ x_i v D_i.(x_i,v) \ $ and if
$dom(\rho)=X$ we refer to $\rho$ as a total assignment.

We say that a total assignment $\rho$ is valid, if it
satisfies all the rules which is denoted as $\rho \models F$.

A partial assignment $\rho', dom(\rho') \subseteq X$ is
valid if there is at least one total assignment $ 
 '$ that is valid $ F$, i.e. if there is
at least one way to successfully finish the existing configuration
process.

 example 
Consider specifying a T-shirt by choosing the color (black, white,
red, or blue), the size (small, medium, or large) and the print
("Men In Black" - MIB or "Save The Whales" - STW). There are two
rules that we have to observe: if we choose the MIB print then the
color black has to be chosen as well, and if we choose the small
size then the STW print (including a big picture of a whale)
cannot be selected as the large whale does not fit on the small
shirt. The configuration problem $(X,D,F)$ of the T-shirt example
consists of variables $X = \{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ representing color,
size and print. Variable domains are $D_1 = \ black , 
white , red , blue \ $, $D_2 = \ small , 
medium , large \ $, and $D_3 = \ MIB , STW \ $. The
two rules translate to $F = \{f_1,f_2\}$, where $f_1 = (x_3 = 
MIB ) (x_1 = black )$ and $f_2 = (x_3 = 
STW ) (x_2 small )$. There are
$|D_1||D_2||D_3| = 24$ possible assignments. Eleven of these
assignments are valid configurations and they form the solution
space shown in Fig.~ . $\Diamond$

sections.content_ko:
인터랙티브 구성 문제에 대한 입력 모델은 제약 조건이 명제 공식으로 표현되는 특별한 종류의 제약 만족 문제(Constraint Satisfaction Problem, CSP)입니다:

정의  
구성 모델 $C$는 변수 집합 $X = \{x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1}\}$, 유한 도메인 $D = D_0 \times D_1 \times \ldots \times D_{n-1}$의 카르테시안 곱, 그리고 원자 명제 $x_i = v$에 대한 명제 공식 집합 $F = \{f_0, \ldots, f_{m-1}\}$로 이루어진 삼중항 $(X,D,F)$입니다. 여기서 $v \in D_i$는 변수의 값에 대한 조건을 지정합니다.  
정의  

구체적으로, 모든 도메인은 $D_i = \{0, 1, \ldots, |D_i|-1\}$로 정의될 수 있습니다. 변수 $x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1}$에 값 $v_0, \ldots, v_{n-1}$을 할당하는 것은 할당 $\rho = (x_0,v_0), \ldots, (x_{n-1},v_{n-1})$로 표기됩니다. 할당의 도메인 $dom(\rho)$는 할당된 변수의 집합입니다: $dom(\rho) = \{x_i \mid v \in D_i\}$. 만약 $dom(\rho) = X$라면 우리는 $\rho$를 전체 할당(total assignment)이라고 부릅니다.

전체 할당 $\rho$가 유효하다고 말할 수 있는 조건은 모든 규칙을 만족해야 하며, 이는 $\rho \models F$로 표기됩니다.

부분 할당 $\rho', dom(\rho') \subseteq X$가 유효하려면, 적어도 하나의 전체 할당 $\rho''$가 존재해야 하며, 이 전체 할당은 $F$를 만족해야 합니다. 즉, 기존 구성 프로세스를 성공적으로 마무리할 수 있는 방법이 적어도 하나는 존재해야 합니다.

예시  
T-셔츠를 지정할 때 색상(검정, 흰색, 빨간색 또는 파란색), 사이즈(작은, 중간 또는 큰) 및 프린트("Men In Black" - MIB 또는 "Save The Whales" - STW)를 선택한다고 가정해 보겠습니다. 우리가 준수해야 할 두 가지 규칙이 있습니다: MIB 프린트를 선택하면 색상으로 검정색도 선택해야 하며, 작은 사이즈를 선택하면 STW 프린트(고래의 큰 그림 포함)를 선택할 수 없습니다. 왜냐하면 큰 고래는 작은 셔츠에 맞지 않기 때문입니다. T-셔츠 예제의 구성 문제 $(X,D,F)$는 색상, 사이즈 및 프린트를 나타내는 변수 $X = \{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$로 구성됩니다. 변수 도메인은 $D_1 = \{검정, 흰색, 빨간색, 파란색\}$, $D_2 = \{작은, 중간, 큰\}$, 그리고 $D_3 = \{MIB, STW\}$입니다. 두 가지 규칙은 $F = \{f_1,f_2\}$로 변환되며, 여기서 $f_1 = (x_3 = MIB) \Rightarrow (x_1 = 검정)$이고 $f_2 = (x_3 = STW) \Rightarrow (x_2 = 작은)$입니다. 가능한 할당의 수는 $|D_1||D_2||D_3| = 24$입니다. 이 중 11개의 할당이 유효한 구성이며, 이들은 Fig.~에 나타난 솔루션 공간을 형성합니다. $\Diamond$
